title: Bourbon Vanilla Tallow Balm: My Weirdly Good Skin Thing
body:
Okay so I saw this stuff online. Beef tallow balm. For your face. I was scrolling, it was late, my hands were cracking from all the hand-washing this spring—seriously, the weather can't decide if it's winter or summer, my skin is just confused and mad about it—and this ad pops up. Whipped Tallow Balm. Bourbon Vanilla scent. Made from grass-fed beef fat. I laughed. Out loud. My dog looked at me. I was like, beef fat? On my skin? That sounds like something my great-grandma would have used before they invented, you know, actual lotion. But the reviews were weirdly good. And my fancy $40 cream from the department store was sitting there doing exactly nothing. So I clicked. I figured, worst case, I'm out thirty bucks and have a funny story. Anyway, that's how I ended up putting beef tallow on my face. And honestly? It's kind of amazing. I don't know how else to say it.

## Why I Even Tried Putting Beef Fat on My Face

Look. I was skeptical. The whole thing felt very... frontier times. Like, churn your own butter, sew your own clothes, render fat for skincare. Not my vibe. I'm a person who buys the nice-smelling stuff in the pretty bottle. But then I started reading. Not deep diving, just like, the product page and a couple articles while waiting for my coffee to brew. And the science-y bit, or the history bit I guess, started to make a weird kind of sense.

So apparently, tallow—that's the fat from around a cow's kidneys, the good stuff from grass-fed cows—is structurally really close to the oils our own skin makes. Like, closer than most plant oils or whatever they put in regular moisturizers. Our skin recognizes it. It doesn't just sit on top like a greasy film; it actually gets in there. It's like giving your skin something it already knows how to use. That was the first "huh" moment. The second was thinking about my grandma. She never had fancy creams. She had a tin of something simple she swore by. I can't remember what it was called, but it was probably just lard or something. Maybe she was onto something we forgot.

And my skin was just so dry. Not cute, dewy dry. More like sandpaper elbows and knuckles that looked like a topographical map. So I ordered the bourbon vanilla one. Because if I'm gonna smear cow fat on myself, it should at least smell nice.

## What This Stuff Is Actually Like

It showed up in a little box. The jar itself is small, heavy glass. Feels substantial. I opened it. The texture is... unique. It's whipped, so it's super light and airy, like cool whip but denser. You scoop a tiny bit with your finger and it just melts. Like, immediately. The temperature of your skin turns it from this fluffy cloud into an oil. It's not greasy. That's the part I can't get over. You rub it in and it's just gone. Your skin feels... quiet. That's the best word. Not slick, not tight, just calm. Hydrated. I used it on my hands first because I was still a chicken about my face.

The smell. Right. Bourbon Vanilla. It's not a bakery vanilla. It's not a candle. It's deeper. Warmer. Like vanilla extract you'd cook with, but smoother. No alcohol smell. Just a cozy, classic vanilla that doesn't scream. It's comforting. It's the kind of smell that makes you take a deep breath. I keep the jar on my nightstand now just for that.

I started using it at night. After I wash my face, I put a little dab on my cheeks, forehead, neck. It sinks in while I read or watch TV. My skin drinks it. In the morning, my face doesn't have that panicked, tight feeling. It just feels normal. Balanced. I've even used it on my lips when they're chapped and it works better than any lip balm I've owned, and I've owned approximately seven hundred. I got a tiny bit on a hangnail once and it was healed in like a day. This stuff is witchcraft.

## My Skin After a Few Weeks of This Experiment

So it's been maybe a month? Six weeks? I don't keep track. But I can tell you what's different. The big one is my hands. They don't look like they've been through a wood chipper anymore. The cracks around my knuckles are gone. My cuticles aren't a mess. I keep the jar by the kitchen sink and slap some on after doing dishes. Game changer.

My face is less... reactive. It used to get red and annoyed if I looked at it wrong. Now it's just chill. I don't have that mid-afternoon urge to splash water on it because it feels tight. The dry patches I used to get around my nose and eyebrows? Gone. Completely. It's not a miracle glow or anything—I still look like me, just a more hydrated version. A version that isn't constantly thinking about her skin. That's the real benefit. I just don't think about it anymore. It's not a problem to solve.

Here's a weirdly specific thing. My elbows. They haven't been this smooth since I was a kid. I didn't even realize how rough they were until they weren't. I showed my mom on the phone last week and she was like "what did you do?" and I had to explain the whole beef tallow thing. She was skeptical too. Then I sent her a jar. She's hooked now. We're a tallow family, I guess.

## Would I Buy This Tallow Balm Again?

Yeah. I already did. I'm halfway through my second jar. I got the bourbon vanilla again because I'm obsessed with the smell. It's my little nighttime ritual. The jar lasts forever because you need so little. A pea-sized amount for your whole face. So the price, which seemed a bit much at first, actually makes sense. It's cheaper per use than the drugstore lotion I was going through every two weeks.

I found it on this little Etsy shop. The person who makes it is in France, I think. Everything is small-batch. You can tell. It feels cared for. I like that. It's the opposite of some giant corporate product in a plastic bottle. This feels like someone took time to make a good thing. That matters to me now, I guess.

If you're curious about natural ingredients and tallow skincare benefits, this is a pretty painless way to try it. It's not scary. It's just a really good balm that happens to be made from grass-fed beef tallow. The weirdness factor wears off after like, two uses. Then you're just left with skin that finally feels okay.

## Quick Questions I Get Asked

**Is beef tallow good for your face?**
Weirdly, yes. Because it's so similar to our skin's own sebum, it absorbs deeply and helps reinforce your skin's barrier. It doesn't just moisturize the surface; it helps your skin help itself. My face has never been happier or less fussy.

**Does tallow balm clog pores?**
Not in my experience. And I'm prone to clogged pores. Because it absorbs so completely and mimics your natural oils, it doesn't sit on top and gunk things up. It's the opposite. It seems to balance everything out. My skin is clearer now than when I was using "non-comedogenic" gels.

**What does the Bourbon Vanilla tallow balm smell like?**
It's a warm, cozy vanilla. Not sweet or sugary. More like the vanilla bean itself, deep and comforting. It's not overpowering. It just smells nice and clean and makes you feel like you're doing something good for yourself. It's the best part of my night, honestly.

Anyway. If your skin is being difficult, or you're just tired of products that don't do what they promise, this might be worth a shot. It was for me. My skin's happy, I'm happy. That's all I wanted.
